tour.title: Historic Istanbul: Hippodrome to the Golden Horn
tour.summary: Three thousand years of empire in three kilometres — and a ferry to Asia at the end.
tour.difficulty: Easy. Flat, paved and pedestrian for almost the entire route, with cobbles and gentle slopes near the palace.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Early morning, around 9am, before the square fills and while the light is soft on the domes.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Individual credits appear under each stop's photograph.

stops.name: Obelisk of Theodosius
stops.entranceFeeNote: It stands in the open on Sultanahmet Square. No ticket, no gate, open at all hours.
stops.accessibility: Level paved ground, step free from the square. The reliefs on the base are low and hard to see from a wheelchair.
stops.insiderTip: Look at the four corners of the marble base. The scenes are different on each face, and the one on the north side shows the obelisk being winched upright.
stops.nextStopDirections: Stay on the square and walk roughly twenty metres further south, along the same line of monuments. The next stop is the bronze column, and you will see it slightly to your right.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Apaleutos25, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Serpentine Column
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open monument on the square. The surviving serpent head is in the Istanbul Archaeological Museum, which charges its own ticket.
stops.accessibility: Right beside the paved path with level access.
stops.insiderTip: The column is hollow and was once a fountain, with water spouting from the mouths of the three snakes.
stops.nextStopDirections: Continue south along the line of monuments for about thirty metres. The third stop, a tall column built from rough stone blocks, is directly ahead of you.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Apaleutos25, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Obelisk of Constantine
stops.insiderTip: This is the southern end of the old racetrack. From here you can see how long the Hippodrome was, which is hard to judge from the middle.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn around and walk back north along the square, past the Egyptian obelisk and the bronze column, for about two hundred and fifty metres. Keep the Blue Mosque on your right. The German Fountain is at the far north end of the square, an ornate domed structure you cannot miss.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Apaleutos25, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: German Fountain
stops.entranceFeeNote: Open to walk around and inside the colonnade.
stops.accessibility: Steps up to the fountain platform on one side, ramped approach on the other.
stops.insiderTip: Step inside and look straight up: the ceiling mosaics are gold and almost nobody looks, with the sultan's calligraphic signature and the Kaiser's crowned W alternating around the dome. The fountain also stands on grim ground. This was the site of the Vakvak plane tree, from which rebellious soldiers hung senior officials in 1656, earning it the name Bloody Plane.
stops.nextStopDirections: Turn right and walk about two hundred metres south east, along the side of the square. The Blue Mosque is the huge building with six minarets in front of you. Head for the main visitor entrance, which faces the square rather than the park.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: A.Savin, FAL, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Blue Mosque
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free for worshippers and visitors. No ticket and no booking. Ignore anyone at the door offering to sell you entry.
stops.openingHours: Open to visitors from about 08:30 until around dusk, but closed to tourists during each of the five daily prayers, roughly 60 to 90 minutes each time. On Fridays it is closed to visitors until about 14:30. Prayer times shift daily, so check the day's timetable.
stops.accessibility: Step free route through the visitor entrance with a ramp. Headscarves are provided at the door and shoes are removed, so bring socks.
stops.insiderTip: The visitor entrance is on the square side, not the park side. If a long queue has formed, walk around to the courtyard on the far side, which is usually quicker and where you must enter anyway.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the mosque by the courtyard and walk north east, away from the Hippodrome, for about three hundred metres. You are heading towards the tram tracks and Hagia Sophia. The bathhouse is a long low building with domes, on your left just before you reach the square in front of Hagia Sophia.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Pedro Szekely from Los Angeles, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Ayasofya Haseki Hürrem Baths
stops.entranceFeeNote: Not a museum: a working luxury hammam priced in euros. Packages run 110 EUR for 45 minutes, 155 EUR for 60, 220 EUR for 80 and 300 EUR for 110 minutes, roughly 6,100 to 16,600 TL. The lira figure moves with the exchange rate, so verify with the operator.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 07:00 to 24:00 in summer and 08:00 to 22:00 in winter. Reservations are strongly advised, particularly for evening slots.
stops.accessibility: The exterior is fully visible from the pavement. The historic interior has uneven heated marble and is not step free.
stops.insiderTip: This is a working hamam, not a museum. If you book, ask for a traditional scrub and foam wash rather than a massage package.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk on another two hundred metres towards Hagia Sophia. Just before you reach it, turn left down the side street where you will see a small sign for Yerebatan. The entrance to the cistern is on your right after about fifty metres.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gryffindor, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Basilica Cistern
stops.entranceFeeNote: Foreign adult daytime ticket 1,950 TL, per an official Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality notice of 3 February 2026. Turkish citizens pay 450 TL. Evening sessions, 19:30 to 22:00, cost 3,000 TL. Under sevens free. Turkish museum prices change often, so verify before you travel.
stops.openingHours: Open daily. Daytime visits run roughly 09:00 to 18:30, with a separate evening session from 19:30 to 22:00. Queues peak between 10:00 and 15:00, and the ticket costs more at night.
stops.accessibility: A long staircase leads down and back up, with no lift. The walkway inside is flat but can be slippery and is often crowded.
stops.insiderTip: Book a timed slot online in high season. The queue without a ticket regularly runs to an hour, and the inside is far quieter in the first hour after opening.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come back up to street level and turn right. Walk about two hundred metres along the tram line, and Hagia Sophia will be directly in front of you, a large pink building with a great dome and four minarets. Head for the visitor entrance on the square side.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Hagia Sophia Mosque
stops.entranceFeeNote: Foreign visitors pay about 25 EUR for the upper-gallery route. The fee is set in euros, not lira, so the lira equivalent moves daily. Worshippers entering to pray are not charged. Children under eight enter free with a passport. Istanbul museum passes do not cover Hagia Sophia.
stops.openingHours: Open to tourists daily, generally 09:00 to 19:30, opening at 08:00 from April to September. Closed to visitors during all five daily prayers. On Fridays the closure is longest, roughly 12:00 to 14:30, for the weekly congregational prayer. Last entry is well before closing, so do not arrive late.
stops.accessibility: Step free entry at the visitor gate with some uneven historic flooring inside. The upper gallery is reached by a steep ramp and is not accessible to wheelchairs.
stops.insiderTip: The interior is brightest in the afternoon, when the sun comes through the south windows and the mosaics in the apse are at their best. Enter with shoulders and knees covered.
stops.nextStopDirections: With your back to Hagia Sophia, walk to the right and up the slope towards the large stone gate with the fountain in front of it. It is about two hundred metres, gently uphill. That gate is the entrance to Topkapı Palace.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Adli Wahid, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Topkapı Palace Museum
stops.entranceFeeNote: Combined ticket covering palace, Harem and Hagia Irene: 2,750 TL for foreign visitors. Bought separately the Harem is 1,050 TL, so the combined ticket is better value. Turkish citizens pay 500 TL and Turkish students 100 TL. These figures come from an independent visitor guide, not the ministry site, so treat them as a strong indication and verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Open daily except Tuesday, 09:00 to 18:00, with the ticket office closing at 17:00. Closed on the first day of Ramadan Bayram and on 1 January. Last entry to the Harem is earlier than the palace closing time.
stops.accessibility: The first and second courtyards are step free. The third and fourth courtyards and the harem involve steps and uneven cobbles, and the harem is not wheelchair accessible.
stops.insiderTip: Go straight to the treasury and the sacred relics first, then work backwards. The tour groups all start at the same end and the queue for the relics can reach forty minutes by mid morning.
stops.nextStopDirections: Do not go through the gate. Turn around and walk back downhill, then take the first narrow lane on your right, which runs along the palace wall. This is Soğukçeşme Street, and it begins about thirty metres along on your right.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Carlos Delgado, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Soğukçeşme Street
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public street. The cafes and the hotel are private businesses.
stops.openingHours: Open at all times. It is a residential lane, so keep noise down early and late.
stops.accessibility: Pedestrian only and mostly level, with cobbles and a gentle slope at the lower end.
stops.insiderTip: Walk to the bottom of the street and turn round for the classic view, with the timber houses on both sides and the palace wall closing the top of the frame.
stops.nextStopDirections: Follow the street down to the bottom and turn left along the main road. Walk about three hundred metres, passing the entrance to the archaeological museum on your right. The main gate of Gülhane Park is on your right, a short way past the museum.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gryffindor, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Gülhane Park
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free admission to the park. The Museum of the History of Science and Technology in Islam, inside the park, charges a separate modest ticket.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, broadly dawn until late evening, around 06:00 to 22:00 in summer with shorter hours in winter. Hours vary by season, so verify at the gate.
stops.accessibility: Main paths are wide and paved with gentle gradients. Some side paths and the area around the Goths' Column are steep and uneven.
stops.insiderTip: The tea garden at the northern end sits on the old palace walls with a view over the Bosphorus. It is cheap and it is the best view on the whole walk.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the park by the main gate and turn right along the tram line. Walk west for about three hundred and fifty metres, keeping the tram tracks on your left. Cross towards the small mosque and the lanes behind Sirkeci station. That cluster of streets is Hoca Paşa.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Maurice Flesier, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Hoca Paşa
stops.entranceFeeNote: Public neighbourhood, no ticket. Expect to pay for food and drink only.
stops.openingHours: Always open. Lunchtime is the best moment, when the lokantas are full of local office workers.
stops.accessibility: Narrow pavements and some steep side streets. Main routes through are paved.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the handwritten menu taped in the window and a queue of men in shirtsleeves at midday. That is the test for a good lokanta around here.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north west for about five hundred metres, crossing the main road towards the water. You are heading for a large stone building with a row of domes along its roof. The spice bazaar entrance is on the far side, next to the mosque.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Martin Dürrschnabel, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Egyptian Bazaar
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter; you pay only for what you buy. Bargaining is expected, and opening prices are often a third to a half above what a seller will accept.
stops.openingHours: Open every day including Sunday, roughly 08:00 to 19:30 Monday to Saturday and from about 09:30 on Sundays. Closed on the main days of Ramadan Bayram and Kurban Bayram. Note that the Grand Bazaar, unlike this one, shuts all day Sunday.
stops.accessibility: Level entrance from the waterfront side and a paved floor. The lanes are narrow and very crowded, which is the main difficulty rather than steps.
stops.insiderTip: Walk to the far end and use the exit by the New Mosque, then look back at the building from outside. The L shape and the domes make much more sense from there than from inside.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the waterfront exit and walk towards the water. The ferry terminals are directly ahead of you, about a hundred metres away, along with the bridges over the Golden Horn.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Robot8A, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Eminönü
stops.entranceFeeNote: Public waterfront, no ticket. Ferries, food and the Galati Bridge are pay-as-you-go. An Istanbulkart is the cheapest way onward.
stops.openingHours: Always open. Ferries run from early morning until around 11pm, most frequently at commuter hours.
stops.accessibility: Wide level promenade with step free access to the ferry piers, though boarding a moving ferry can be difficult for some visitors.
stops.insiderTip: Buy an Istanbulkart from the machines by the piers, then take the short crossing to Kadıköy. Sit on the right hand side going out for the best view of the old city skyline.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is the final stop. The walk ends here at the waterfront, with the ferry piers in front of you and the Galata Bridge to your left. If you want to continue, the Spice Bazaar is behind you and the Galata Tower is across the bridge, about twenty minutes on foot.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jorge Láscar from Australia, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
